description: Military and strategic theory of space: spacepower, astropolitics, deterrence
Treaties, national laws, COPUOS, Artemis Accords, property rights, safety zones
IR theory, critical and colonial readings, polycentric governance
Expansion ethics, existential risk, settlement sovereignty, futures methods
Science fiction and expert foresight as hypothesis sources
Orbital mechanics, light-lag, solar gradient, gravity wells as strategic facts
Deposits, evidence grades, extraction, ISRU
Energy and propulsion ladder: solar, fission, fusion, electric and nuclear propulsion
Machine-first expansion, autonomy levels, material closure
Launch prices, learning curves, reusability
Propellant, servicing and logistics markets in space; price formation; backstop pricing
Earth markets for space-sourced goods: PGMs, helium-3, rare earths; price response
Orbital congestion, debris, orbit-use fees, slot and spectrum allocation
Returns to space R&D, technology transfer, multipliers
Whether and where space activity pays; anchor demand; the post-Apollo stall
Government as anchor customer, contract structures (cost-plus, fixed-price, COTS)
Venture capital, IPOs, investor theses, failures of space ventures
Space insurance market, loss rates, risk pricing
Space-economy size estimates and their definitions
History of spaceflight and of earlier exploration ventures (VOC, chartered companies)
Cold-start and coordination problems, subsidies and incentive design (tokenomics parallels)
Earth market prices, supply and demand of goods a space economy could supply or replace
Price and income elasticities of demand and supply; substitution
Launchers, reuse, payload, flight rate, prices
Landers and surface delivery: performance, prices, outcomes
Habitats, construction from regolith, surface infrastructure
Surface and spacecraft power: solar, fission, storage
Life support, closure of air and water loops, crew systems
Wargaming, game theory, agent-based models, operations research applied to space
